body:
## What

Two changes to the BSON reader (`binary_reader.hpp`). They speed up `from_bson()` and BSON `sax_parse()` and leave behaviour unchanged.

- **Terminators 8 bytes at a time.** `get_bson_cstr_bulk()` (contiguous input) looked for the `0x00` that ends a key one byte at a time. It now calls the new `find_zero_byte()` in `string_scan.hpp`, which tests 8 bytes per step with the same SWAR zero-byte test the lexer's string scanners use (`(v - 0x01…) & ~v & 0x80…`, first hit via `count_trailing_zeros`).
- **Array element names are skipped.** BSON names an array's elements `"0"`, `"1"`, … These names are never passed to the SAX parser, yet each one was copied into the key string and run through `check_string_utf8()`. They are now skipped without being copied. The exception is `error_handler_t::strict`, which still reads and checks them, so ill-formed UTF-8 in an element name is rejected exactly as before (same `parse_error.113`, same byte position). `replace`/`ignore` only ever sanitised a string that was then thrown away, so nothing observable changes for them.

This came out of a research session on whether the SIMD/SWAR techniques used for JSON text apply to the binary formats. BSON's NUL-terminated names are one of the few remaining byte scans in CBOR/BSON. More PRs (CBOR runs of scalars, strict-mode UTF-8, BSON writer size pass) may follow.

## Measurements

Paired A/B with my local harness (both variants in one binary, alternating samples, two link orders), A = `develop` (755bb16d7a), B = this PR, nativejson-benchmark files converted with `to_bson()`. The workload runs `from_bson()` and `sax_parse()` on each file.

Instructions per parse (B/A):

| case | Mac, Apple clang 21 | VPS x86-64, GCC 13 (callgrind) |
|---|---|---|
| SAX twitter | 0.908 | 0.918 |
| SAX citm_catalog | 0.892 | 0.906 |
| SAX canada | 0.684 | 0.749 |
| `from_bson` twitter | 0.973 | 0.980 |
| `from_bson` citm_catalog | 0.972 | 0.977 |
| `from_bson` canada | 0.904 | 0.910 |
| `from_bson` citm_catalog, `strict` | 0.994 | 0.999 |
| `from_bson` citm_catalog, `std::istringstream` | 0.942 | 0.983 |

Timings (Mac, geomean over both link orders, 64-byte function alignment) are within noise or better in every row: `from_bson` canada 0.856, citm 0.950, twitter 0.955; SAX citm 0.858, twitter 0.904. SAX canada with a non-virtual SAX handler is flat in time (1.006) despite −32 % instructions. With a `json_sax`-derived (virtual) handler it goes from 2.76 to 2.09 ms. No VPS timings were taken.

## Tests

- `BSON keys from contiguous and stream input` now also has keys of 1 to 17 bytes and arrays of 12 elements, so names end at every position in an 8-byte word. Every truncation of that document is still compared between contiguous and stream input.
- New `BSON array element names`: an element name with an ill-formed byte and one longer than 8 bytes. `keep`/`replace`/`ignore` and stream input accept the document, and `strict` rejects it with the message and position it had before. Both test cases also pass against `develop`'s headers.
- Full suite with ASan/UBSan (`ctest`, 184 tests) passes locally.

## Breaking changes

None. No public API, ABI tag or output changes. The only internal signature changes are in private members of `binary_reader`, plus a new `detail::find_zero_byte()`.

comments.body: Ugh, wasn't fast enough finding this review.

review_comments.body: Split store and validate?  strict only requires validate, not store, for array indices.
review_comments.diff_hunk:
@@ -489,14 +491,18 @@ class binary_reader
     @brief Parses a C-style string from the BSON input.
     @param[in,out] result  A reference to the string variable where the read
                             string is to be stored.
+    @param[in] store  whether the characters are needed; if not (the names of
+                      an array's elements), they are skipped and @a result may
+                      be left unchanged, and they are not checked against
+                      @ref error_handler
     @return `true` if the \\x00-byte indicating the end of the string was
              encountered before the EOF; false` indicates an unexpected EOF.
     */
-    bool get_bson_cstr(string_t& result)
+    bool get_bson_cstr(string_t& result, const bool store = true)

review_comments.body: Is this not a function that existed already?

Right: with `error_handler_t::strict`, the names of array elements are only checked, but the caller passes `store = true` so that `check_string_utf8` has a string to look at. The bulk path could check the bytes in place with `valid_utf8_string(data, length)` instead. I left it as is: it only matters in strict mode, the names are a few bytes ("0", "1", ...), and `key` keeps its capacity between elements, so the copy costs next to nothing. The doc comment of `store` is imprecise, though: in strict mode the names of array elements *are* checked, because they are stored.

*(Written by Claude Code on behalf of @nlohmann.)*

review_comments.body:
No, `find_zero_byte` is new in this PR; nothing searched for a zero byte before. But the idiom inside it, `(x - ones) & ~x & high` for "this word contains byte c", now appears several times in `string_scan.hpp` (`swar_string_special`, `find_zero_byte`, `find_ascii_copyable_run`, `find_string_delimiter`). It could become a small helper in a later cleanup.

*(Written by Claude Code on behalf of @nlohmann.)*

I know that there have been some tests with larger arrays, so while it's not a lot individually, it could add up, and this is a performance series.  It would be a simple change to be `get_bson_cstr(string_t& result, const bool store, const bool validate)` and then pass `store` to `get_bson_cstr_bulk` and use `validate` instead of `store` before `check_string_utf8`.

Then 
```
            if (JSON_HEDLEY_UNLIKELY(!get_bson_cstr(key, is_object || error_handler == error_handler_t::strict)))
```
is
```
            if (JSON_HEDLEY_UNLIKELY(!get_bson_cstr(key, is_object, is_object || error_handler == error_handler_t::strict)))
```
Not a big deal either way, just sharing my original thought process.

review_comments.body:
You were right, and it adds up more than I thought. I measured strict mode on an array of 1M int32 values: skipping the copy and checking the name in place makes the reader 29–36 % faster on x86 (clang 18 / GCC 13) and 28–33 % faster on arm64.

The exact change you sketched can't work as is: if `store` is false, the bytes never reach `result`, so `check_string_utf8(result, "key")` would check an empty string. The check has to run on the input bytes (`valid_utf8_string(data, length)`). I also tried the extra `validate` parameter on `get_bson_cstr`, but that pushed `get_bson_cstr_bulk` over clang's inlining threshold and made the default `keep` path 7.6 % slower on x86. So #5984 adds a separate `check_bson_cstr` for the strict case and leaves `get_bson_cstr` unchanged.

*(Written by Claude Code on behalf of @nlohmann.)*

title: BSON reader: find C-string terminators 8 bytes at a time, skip array element names
